1:
Gill (reformed) fixes the moment: the plague had ceased, and this further confirms the priesthood in Aaron’s family. Henry (puritan-evangelical) notes that the word for a rod is also the word for a tribe, and draws two conclusions from the princes being willing to contend at all. The priesthood was a preferment worth striving for, and serving God is an honour to the greatest of men — though he suspects these men wanted its profit and power rather than what was divine in it. He is struck too that after all that had been done to settle the question men were still ready to reopen it: they strive with God for the dominion, and the question is whose will shall stand. Calvin (reformed) explains why the matter could not be left open. The sacrifices belonged to the whole people, yet God would have them offered by one man in one place: partly because altars everywhere would corrupt his worship by sheer variety, partly to point the people toward the Mediator, since no offering is legitimate but by his grace.

How many rods there were is the first real dispute, and it turns on a tribe. Ellicott (grammatical-historical) sets out both options — that Aaron’s rod was additional to the twelve, or that Ephraim and Manasseh together supplied one — and prefers the second as better suited to the wording, citing Deuteronomy 27:12, where Joseph stands for both and Levi is counted among the twelve. Keil (grammatical-historical) reaches it independently. Calvin is blunter, saying those are mistaken who add a thirteenth rod for Levi, and gives a reason the others do not: Joseph was divided in two only where land was being allotted, whereas here nothing turns on territory, and the contest is between all the other tribes and Levi alone. He adds that Aaron’s rod being in the midst of them is ordinary Hebrew for mingled among them, said expressly so that the ungodly should have no ground to cavil.

Why the name written was Aaron’s rather than Levi’s draws a threefold agreement. Gill points out that a tribal name would have decided nothing, the quarrel lying chiefly between the Levites and Aaron’s family within the same tribe. Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) presses it further: one might have expected two rods for Levi, one for Aaron and one for his competitors, but the single name settled which tribe and which family the dignity belonged to. Ellicott supplies the genealogical reason: Aaron came of Levi’s second son and so was the appointed rather than the natural head of his father’s house, and was made head of priests and Levites alike.

On the rods themselves Wesley is most concrete. Not every person brings one but every tribe, and the rod is the staff a prince carried as the token of his dignity; the name written is each prince’s, since as firstborn and chief they had the strongest claim if the priesthood were open to their tribes, and since each stood for his whole tribe the trial decided the question completely. He infers something about the quarrel behind the chapter: not only Korah and the Levites but men of other tribes had been contending, on the ground that the whole congregation was holy. Ellicott notes that inscribing a name on a rod followed an Egyptian practice, and that a similar sign was required of the prophet at Ezekiel 37:16. Keil translates the promise attached to the rods by the causative force of its verb — to make sink, to bring to rest — so that what the blossoming rod accomplishes is the quieting of the murmuring. Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) says why something further was needed: the dispute had to be settled for good, and this method had the desired effect, the Aaronic priesthood never being questioned after.
8:
Henry (puritan-evangelical) describes what was found and why it settled the matter. The rods were produced before the people, and while every other remained as it was, Aaron’s alone — a dry stick — had become a living branch, with buds in one place, blossoms in another and fruit in a third at the same moment. That simultaneity removes the suspicion of fraud, since no ordinary branch bears all three at once and no substituted bough could have been passed off in the night. Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) makes the same point and then reads the stages: the buds of good desire, the blossoms of resolution and profession, and the ripe fruit of faith and love and obedience, all traced to the priesthood of Christ. Henry keeps it plainer — the sign marked Aaron as under a blessing that yields increase where no man has planted or watered.

Both of the witnesses who know the tree stop on its name, and give it different senses. Clarke thinks the staff was of the common almond, which grows to twenty feet in good soil, flowers a delicate red, and buds in January; its Hebrew name, he says, comes from a root meaning to awake, because it wakes earlier than other trees. Ellicott (grammatical-historical) derives the same name from the cognate verb to keep watch, and explains it by the tree blossoming while the rest of the vegetation lies in the sleep of winter, pointing to the play on the word at Jeremiah 1:11. He also corrects the rendering: not that the rod yielded almonds but that it brought them to maturity.

Ellicott then reads the miracle forward. As the budding rod proved the priesthood in Aaron and his posterity, so Christ proved himself the true High Priest by coming as a rod out of the stem of Jesse at Isaiah 11:1; and the dry stick shooting is a type of how the Spirit works in the Church and its ministry, not by might nor by power, as Zechariah 4:6 has it. A smaller question divides two of the others. Gill (reformed) says Moses went where none but he might go at any time; Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) says the place was closed to all but the high priest, and he once a year, so Moses entered safely only under an express command.

What was to become of the rod afterwards raises a difficulty Ellicott handles carefully. He renders the order as put back, literally make to return, and points out that the text does not say the rod was placed inside the ark, any more than it is said of the pot of manna; neither was in the ark when it came into Solomon’s temple at 1 Kings 8:9. He denies that this conflicts with Hebrews 9:4, since a statement about the ark’s contents at that date does not settle what was in it earlier, and may even hint that something had been. He adds a Jewish tradition that when the ark was hidden the rod and the pot of manna were hidden with it, and that the rod still bore buds and almonds. Calvin (reformed) asks instead why it was kept at all, and answers from the people rather than the object: men are slow to consider God’s works and bury the memory of them as though deliberately, so the sign is laid up and the reason given is their perverseness — which is a reproach. Yet he finds fatherly pity in the same act, since a people so given to rebellion would have provoked wrath again, and God forestalls them to keep them alive. In humbling us, Calvin says, he does not only punish what we have done but has regard to what is good for us, and so proves that he cares for us.
12:
The chapter ends not in submission but in panic, and Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) catches the swing of it. The verb behind their cry, he says, denotes not simply dying but an extreme difficulty of breathing which ends in suffocation, and the sentiment matches the word. These are the people who had lately held that every man among them was holy enough to come near God and minister in holy things; now not one of them dares approach the tabernacle at all without expecting to be consumed. Both positions were wrong, and by the same mistake: some might approach and some might not, God having put the difference, and his decision should have been final with them. Sinners, Clarke concludes, are ever running into extremes. Gill (reformed) makes the same contrast from the other end — men who had thought the priesthood common to them with Aaron are now frightened by the rod laid up against them into supposing they must keep away from the tabernacle entirely.

Calvin (reformed) weighs the fear rather than the facts, and will not simply approve it. To be alarmed by God’s power is somewhat better than to despise it in brutal stupidity, but there is a middle ground between torpor and consternation, and this is not it. Believers do tremble at God’s judgments, and the further a man has advanced in piety the more he feels the divine anger; yet that fear humbles him in such a way that he still seeks after God, whereas the reprobate tremble in a manner that makes them fretfully wish God further off. Israel, stunned by a severity they thought excessive, could only deplore their lot, and because they had no sense of his goodness the chastisement was to them a gibbet rather than a medicine — as though such rigour were not meant to make them more heedful. Calvin allows that this servile fear does sometimes prepare men for repentance, without conceding that it is repentance. Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) reads the cry more sympathetically, as consternation arising from three things together: the memory of judgments severe and repeated, the threat of death on any further murmuring, and a sense of their own guilt and weakness which made them afraid of relapsing into the same faults and bringing the vengeance down again.

The last clause is disputed in form. Wesley takes it as a question, and paraphrases it as asking whether God will proceed with them in strict justice until the whole people is cut off; on the preceding words he notes only that coming near means nearer than a man should, an error easily committed. Gill reports that the Syriac and Arabic render the clause affirmatively — we are about to be consumed — with a Targum to the same effect, and prefers that reading on the ground that it sits better with what has just been said, since men who have already declared they are perishing would scarcely turn the same thought into a question.
